newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania cauldron will bubble even after poll.
newsitem.headline: Albania cauldron will bubble even after poll.

text.p: Expectations hinging on Albania's general election on Sunday seem unrealistically high as few signs exist that law and order will quickly return once the ballots are counted.

Europe, spurred on by the concerns of Italy and Greece over a flood of illegal immigrants, moved relatively quickly to send in troops in April after nearly a month of anarchy sparked by the collapse of pyramid savings schemes.
The presence of nearly 7,000 foreign soldiers did much to calm civilians in Tirana and many other towns and helped to reduce widespread looting and general mayhem.
But the troops are few and there appears to be little appetite among foreign governments to renew the mandate of the "Alba" mission beyond mid-August. But they may have no choice.
Even in the event of a moderately fair election, neither Albanian leaders nor international envoys have come up with any answer on how to halt lawlessness in the south of the country.
Warlords and gangs filled the vacuum left by the departure of army and police, who still lack the punch to venture back into hostile territory.
A senior Western diplomat said on Friday that the two most serious post-election problems were security and the regulation of those savings schemes still in operation.
Any move to control the funds may spark a fresh round of violence from investors, but the economy will remain hostage until the problem is solved.
"No one wanted to tackle this before the election. But can they close these schemes without unleashing more violence?" the diplomat said.
The 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) is overseeing the elections but the running of the polls is in the hands of the 10-party unity government.
OSCE special envoy Franz Vranitzky said the polls were being held in unusual circumstances and would be complex -- a state of emergency imposed on March 2 is still in force.
Indeed, the risks are high and the pitfalls many.
One concern the OSCE appears not to have considered publicly is the turnout. Can the election enjoy legitimacy if, say, only 30 percent of the electorate bother to vote?
Electoral registers, many of them destroyed in town halls torched in the unrest in March, could also be called into doubt by any of the parties.
"It would be fair to say already that there are several areas in which it would be difficult to say that this is a normal election," OSCE election coordinator Tony Welch said.

Around 600 observers from the OSCE, the Council of Europe and the United States are taking up position across the country to monitor the vote on Sunday. They want to prevent the massive manipulation of the last general election 13 months ago.
But there is doubt they will see much of what will go on in the 4,525 polling stations. OSCE officials say they will concentrate in key areas and be present in at least 250 counts.
"Ballot stuffing and the count are still potential problems," one diplomat said.
Most importantly, will the parties, in particular President Sali Berisha's Democrats and their rival Socialists, respect the result if it does not suit their expectations?
Both parties have already complained that they have been prevented from campaigning in some areas by rival supporters.

Sources close to Berisha, who insists he will accept the results if backed by the OSCE, have told diplomats privately that he will step down if the left wins power. But if the vote is close, he will probably remain.
"I think it will be fairly close and with Berisha in power it'll be difficult for Albania to move ahead," one envoy said.
A member of the European Parliament was more pessimistic. She said if the election failed to restore stability, Albania could become 'the Medellin of Europe'.
